This principle—dubbed the “one-bite” doctrine because it permits the 
agency only one bite at the interpretive apple—originated in dicta in 
Paralyzed Veterans (and thus came to be dubbed the “Paralyzed Veterans 
doctrine” even though it was only one of several proposition for which 
Paralyzed Veterans stood) and was then actually applied by the D.C. 
Circuit in a series of cases until the Supreme Court granted certiorari in 
one of them. In Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association, 135 S.Ct. 1199 
(2015), a unanimous Supreme Court disapproved the one-bite doctrine as 
inconsistent with the APA § 553, which exempts all interpretive rules from 
notice and comment, with no carve-out for those that alter a prior 
interpretive rule. However, the Court said nothing new about the far more 
common question of how to distinguish an interpretive rule from a 
legislative rule to begin with. Instead the Justices merely said that the 
term interpretive rule
is not further defined by the APA, and its precise meaning is the 
source of much scholarly and judicial debate. We need not, and do 
not, wade into that debate here. For our purposes, it suffices to 
say that the critical feature of interpretive rules is that they are 
“issued by an agency to advise the public of the agency’s 
construction of the statutes and rules which it administers.” 
Shalala v, Guernsey Memorial Hospital, 514 U.S. 87, 99 (1995) 
(internal quotation marks omitted). The absence of a notice-and- 
comment obhgation makes the process of issuing interpretive 
rules comparatively easier for agencies than issuing legislative 
rules. But that convenience comes at a price: Interpretive rules 
“do not have the force and effect of law and are not accorded that 
weight in the adjudicatory process.” Ibid.
* *  
While the one-bite doctrine was rejected by the Supreme Court, the 
ideas in the remainder of the Paralyzed Veterans opinion—^about how to 
distinguish interpretive rules from legislative rules in the first place on the 
basis of the relationship between such rules and the preexisting legal 
authorities they purport to interpret—^remain central to D.C. Circuit 
decisionmaking, as reflected in the following case.
Note that Paralyzed Veterans did not apply this reasoning to interpretive rules that 
purport to construe a statute rather than a legislative rule.
